summary: This informational memo describes the encryption and key management used by GigaBeam in its WiFiber family of radio link products. It was documented in the hope that other wireless product efforts will include comparable security.

eli5.summary: A company explains how it locks the messages sent over its high-speed radio links, hoping other companies will lock theirs just as well.

subtitle: Encryption and key management for GigaBeam's high-speed point-to-point radio links.

tldr.problem: GigaBeam's WiFiber radio links can transmit over a gigabit per second through the air over distances of about a mile. Because radio signals can be intercepted, some customers need confidentiality and integrity protection.
tldr.mechanism: GigaBeam uses AES-GCM encryption with a custom security protocol for subscriber traffic, AES-CBC and HMAC-SHA-1 with IPsec for management traffic, and IKE with RSA signatures for key management between the two radio control modules.
tldr.outcome: The documented solution allows customers to protect high-speed wireless data without the overhead of full IPsec, and serves as a model for other wireless product developers.

facts.label: Encryption algorithm
facts.value: AES-GCM for traffic, AES-CBC for management

today: RFC 4705 is an Informational document describing the encryption and key management used by GigaBeam in its WiFiber product family as of 2006. It was published in hopes of encouraging other wireless product vendors to implement comparable security features.

sections.title: GigaBeam High-Speed Radio Links
sections.content:
GigaBeam WiFiber is a product family providing point-to-point radio links that transmit over gigabit per second at distances of about a mile. The beam width is less than one degree, which makes eavesdropping harder than with broadcast radio: an attacker must be nearly between the transmitter and receiver, or directly behind the receiver. However, interception is still possible, so GigaBeam designed a security solution.

The radio link appears to the network devices at each end as if they were connected by a fiber optic cable. Gigabit Ethernet traffic goes in one end, and Gigabit Ethernet traffic comes out the other end, with the air link in between. The Radio Control Module (RCM) at each end converts the Ethernet encoding, applies encryption, adds error correction, and transmits the data as radio frames.
sections.eli5: GigaBeam sells a radio link that sends data really fast through the air and looks like a fiber cable to the devices using it. They built encryption into it so people cannot listen in.

sections.title: Radio Link Frame Structure
sections.content:
Each GigaBeam radio link frame is 2240 bits long and contains:

  • SYNC (11 bits): Synchronization pattern for the receiver to find the start of the frame
  • KEYSEL (1 bit): Indicates which of two encryption keys was used, allowing seamless key rotation
  • PN (40 bits): Packet number, a counter that increments for each frame; required by AES-GCM
  • FLAGS (28 bits): Control bits indicating which data blocks contain control codes rather than data
  • DCC (8 bits): Data Communications Channel, used for management protocol traffic between the radio control modules
  • DATA (1792 bits): Encrypted subscriber data, 28 blocks of data
  • TAG (96 bits): Authentication tag from AES-GCM, truncated to 96 bits
  • SPARE (24 bits): Reserved for future use
  • CHECK (240 bits): Reed-Solomon forward error correction check codes
sections.eli5: Each radio frame is like an envelope with labels for routing and authentication, encrypted data inside, and extra bits for fixing errors and rotating keys.

sections.title: Encryption and Key Management
sections.content:
The GigaBeam RCM contains two key registers, allowing it to switch between an active key and a new key without dropping frames. The KEYSEL field indicates which key was used for each frame.

For subscriber traffic: AES-GCM is used with counter mode. The counter is constructed from a 32-bit salt (provided by IKE), the 40-bit packet number from the frame, and padding. AES-GCM encrypts the DATA field and authenticates both the DATA and FLAGS fields, producing a 96-bit authentication tag.

For management traffic: The 8-bit Data Communications Channel field carries fragments of a Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) link between the two RCMs. IKE runs over this PPP link to manage encryption keys. Other management traffic is protected with IPsec ESP using AES-CBC and HMAC-SHA-1.

Key establishment: IKE Phase 1 uses Aggressive Mode with RSA digital signatures and X.509 certificates to establish a secure channel between the RCMs. Each device generates its own public/private key pair at the factory and has its certificate signed by the GigaBeam Root CA. Phase 1 establishes an ISAKMP Security Association. Phase 2 (Quick Mode) negotiates the actual encryption keys without Perfect Forward Secrecy, as subsequent key rotation occurs frequently.
sections.eli5: Subscriber data gets encrypted with AES-GCM, which also adds a tamper-proof seal. Management traffic gets encrypted with AES-CBC. Two computers set up their encryption keys using IKE with certificates they carry from the factory.

sections.title: Forward Error Correction and Signal Processing
sections.content:
After encryption, the frame goes through several signal processing steps:

Forward Error Correction (FEC): The 224 10-bit symbols making up the frame are grouped into 4 subframes of 56 symbols each using symbol interleaving. A Reed-Solomon code RS(56,50) is applied, which detects 6 errors and corrects 3 errors per subframe. FEC is always active but correction can be disabled for debugging.

Scrambling: A linear feedback shift register with polynomial (1 + x^14 + x^15) scrambles all bits except the SYNC pattern, ensuring that long runs of ones or zeros do not occur. The scrambler initializes to all ones at the start of each frame. This is necessary because during the initial IKE exchange, frames would otherwise be all zeros.

Differential Encoding: The bit stream is differentially encoded to prevent symbol inversion ambiguity at the receiver. A zero bit is encoded as no change, a one bit as a change from the previous bit. This way, if the receiver inverts all bits (due to RF processing), the differential decoding still recovers the right data.
sections.eli5: After encryption, the signal gets triple-protected: error-correcting codes let the receiver fix small damage, scrambling prevents recognizable patterns, and special encoding handles radio signal flips.

sections.title: Security Analysis
sections.content:
The RFC documents several security considerations. AES-GCM uses counter mode, which is very efficient but dangerous if the same counter is used twice with the same key. The key management system prevents this: each frame uses a unique packet number in the counter, and IKE ensures that each security association has a unique salt value.

AES with a 128-bit key provides 2^128 possible keys. The 40-bit packet number means up to 2^40 frames can use a single key before counter exhaustion, well before the security association becomes distinguishable from random at the cryptographic level.

The system uses IKEv1 rather than IKEv2, primarily because an IKEv1 implementation was available for the RCM's processing environment. IKEv2 would provide additional capabilities like Diffie-Hellman group negotiation, but these were not critical for this application.

Keying material and Diffie-Hellman exponents should be erased from memory immediately after use. Periodic full Phase 1 rekeying is recommended to limit exposure if a Diffie-Hellman private key is disclosed.
sections.eli5: The encryption is secure as long as keys never get reused for the same counter value. The system avoids this automatically. Administrators should change keys regularly to be extra safe.

fields.name: KEYSEL
fields.desc: Selects which of two key registers was used for this frame.

fields.name: PN
fields.desc: Packet number, incremented for each frame, used in AES-GCM counter.

fields.name: FLAGS
fields.desc: Control bits, one per 64B/65B data block, indicates control codes.

fields.name: DCC
fields.desc: Data Communications Channel for management protocol traffic.

fields.name: CHECK
fields.desc: Reed-Solomon forward error correction check words.
